outcome: Since 26 January 2024 nothing has settled the conjecture or any case of it with degree two or higher; the in-window events are two unrefereed claims that I could not verify (a May 2025 'symbolic resolution' posted on Cambridge Open Engage, and a June 2025 Preprints.org proof of Schinzel's hypothesis by Huan Xiao, which would settle this problem if valid and whose full text I could not open), together with averaged, analogue and neighbouring results and a Lean formal statement that still contains sorry.
problem_asks: Part 1 (hypotheses, for a given f in Z[x]): (a) the leading coefficient of f is positive; (b) f is irreducible over the integers; (c) there is no common factor of all the values f(x) for positive integers x, i.e. no prime divides every f(x). Part 2 (conclusion): f(x) is prime for infinitely many positive integers x. Part 3 (scope): the assertion is universal, quantified over every f of every degree satisfying (a)-(c). Wikipedia says the conditions are also necessary and the conjecture is that they are sufficient, and it notes that the seemingly weaker statement 'every such f takes a prime value at some positive integer' is equivalent. Degree 1 (Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions) is settled. Degree 2 and higher, for every such f, is what is open, including x^2+1 (Landau's fourth problem).

events.what_happened: Arnaud Bodin, Pierre Debes and Salah Najib, 'The Schinzel Hypothesis for Polynomials' (arXiv:1902.08155). Proves Schinzel's hypothesis H for polynomial rings in place of Z: 'polynomials in at least one variable over the integers, polynomials in several variables over an arbitrary field, etc.' 'Prime' is replaced by irreducible in that setting.
events.delivers: Schinzel's hypothesis for a wide class of polynomial rings, with irreducibility in place of primality. This is an analogue in which the integers are replaced by a polynomial ring, so it does not establish the integer case or the Bunyakovsky statement for any f in Z[x].
events.remains: The integer-ring case, i.e. every item of problem_asks.
events.direction: Supports the Schinzel-type statement in an analogous ring; says nothing for Z.

events.what_happened: Alexei N. Skorobogatov and Efthymios Sofos, 'Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points' (arXiv:2005.02998). Abstract: 'We resolve Schinzel's Hypothesis (H) for 100% of polynomials of arbitrary degree.' The paper applies this to rational points on diagonal conic bundles and generalised Chatelet equations. Published in Inventiones Mathematicae 231(2) (2023), DOI 10.1007/s00222-022-01153-6 (journal details from a search summary, not from the publisher page).
events.revisions: v1 6 May 2020; v2 8 Oct 2020; v3 4 Sep 2022 (current), per arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: A statement about almost all polynomials, in a sense the abstract does not define (the arXiv page I read gives no measure). It covers Schinzel's hypothesis, of which Bunyakovsky's conjecture is the single-polynomial case, for typical polynomials only. For any particular f of degree at least 2, such as t^2+1, the abstract does not establish the statement, since the exceptional set could contain it.
events.remains: Every individual f of degree at least 2, including t^2+1, is not settled by the abstract's statement; the integer case for specific polynomials remains open.

checked_by.qualification: Established journal in the field; I did not verify its referee policy
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, vol. 231 issue 2 (2023), pp. 673-739, per a search summary (not opened)

events.direction: Averaged support for the Schinzel-type statement; neither proves nor refutes any specific case of Bunyakovsky's conjecture.

events.what_happened: Reported only second-hand. A 2025 Portuguese article (Doherty Andrade, JEEPEMA, see andrade-2025-jeepema) cites 'Deloin (2020)' as presenting a proof of the conjecture by a new approach linking it to a general theory of arithmetic progressions; per a search snippet of that article the mathematical community has 'some reservations' about the demonstration. I could not locate Deloin's paper, Deloin's full name, its venue or its text. The article PDF was returned as binary and unreadable to me. The kind value is a placeholder because the publication type is unknown.
events.delivers: Unknown. As reported, a claimed proof of the conjecture or of some case; the scope and hypotheses could not be checked.
events.remains: Unknown; it may be all of problem_asks, or a case of it.
events.doubts: Reservations about the demonstration are reported second-hand in a 2025 article (per a search snippet). I could not read the reservations or the proof.
events.direction: As reported, claims the conjecture (or a case) holds; cannot be confirmed.

events.what_happened: Gareth A. Jones and Alexander K. Zvonkin, 'Block designs and prime values of polynomials' (arXiv:2105.03915). Counted prime values of quadratic polynomials (and cyclotomic polynomials) arising in block-design and permutation-group constructions by Amarra-Devillers-Praeger and by Hujdurovic et al. The counts agree closely with Li's modification of the Bateman-Horn prediction. The paper states that this is not a proof. Published as 'Block designs, permutation groups and prime values of polynomials', Trudy Inst. Mat. Mekh. UrO RAN 29(1) (2023), pp. 233-253 (dates and pages from a search snippet of mathnet.ru).
events.revisions: v1 9 May 2021; v2 4 Jun 2021 (adds computational data, explanatory sections and citations), per arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Nothing toward the conjecture beyond numerical evidence for specific quadratic and cyclotomic polynomials. Finitely many verified instances of a universal claim do not move the problem, and the authors state that the data 'does not prove that these polynomials take infinitely many prime values'.

checked_by.who: Trudy Institute of Mathematics and Mechanics, UrO RAN (journal)
checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed mathematics journal per its name; I did not verify its referee process
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2023 (received 30.09.2021, revised 08.12.2022, accepted 09.12.2022), per a search snippet

events.directly_checkable: The polynomials and their prime-value counts are given in the paper and can be checked by direct computation; the paper does not claim a proof.
events.direction: Evidence for the conjecture in special cases; neither asserts nor refutes it.
events.object: No counterexample. The 'object' is computed data: counts of prime values of specific quadratic and cyclotomic polynomials, with the authors' conclusion that if the conjecture is true each of these polynomials takes infinitely many prime values.

events.what_happened: Valerii Sopin, EasyChair Preprint No. 8203, 'Existence of a Quadratic Polynomial, Which Represents Infinitely Many Prime Numbers' (the version pages show this shared title; one page gives the longer title with 'Bunyakovsky's Conjecture for Degree Greater than One and the 4th Landau Problem'). Abstract: 'No single case of Bunyakovsky's conjecture for degree greater than one has been proved, although numerical evidence in higher degree is consistent with the conjecture. In this paper we overcome such misfortune.' Methods named across versions: Friedlander-Iwaniec theorem, Fermat's two-squares theorem, Brahmagupta-Fibonacci identity, Bezout's lemma, later SL(2,Z) and the hyperbolic prime number theorem. The version page gives four versions; the individual page fetches gave inconsistent single dates, so the dates below are from the versions page.
events.revisions: Per EasyChair versions page: v1 7 Jun 2022; v2 15 Nov 2023 (its note describes a result on infinitely many n for which n^2+1 is prime or a product of two primes); v3 18 Nov 2023 (note: 'the extended Euclidean algorithm'); v4 20 Nov 2023 (note: 'the Hyperbolic Prime Number Theorem'). No version dated inside the window was found.
events.delivers: As the abstract states it: a quadratic polynomial represents infinitely many primes, i.e. the degree-2 case of the conjecture. The v2 version note describes a weaker result, infinitely many n with n^2+1 prime or a product of two primes, which is not the conjecture's conclusion. Which statement the final version proves I could not determine: the PDF was not readable to me. One search summary says the argument concerns f(N)+c for some integer c; I could not confirm this.
events.remains: Every degree-2 polynomial other than the one the paper claims, and every polynomial of degree at least 3. If the paper proves only the almost-prime statement, the prime-value statement for n^2+1 also remains.
events.time_since_posted: About 2 years 11 months since the last version (20 Nov 2023); no public engagement found.
events.doubts: (1) Unrefereed EasyChair preprint. (2) The scope moved between versions: the v2 note describes a weaker almost-prime statement, and later versions add new tools (extended Euclidean algorithm, hyperbolic prime number theorem) without a stated change in claim. (3) The readable pages name no explicit polynomial; the title asserts existence. (4) No review, critique, citation or correction was found in the searches; whether 2025 surveys cite it could not be checked because their reference lists were not readable to me.
events.direction: If the final version proves the prime-value statement for a quadratic, it cuts for the conjecture in degree 2. If it proves only the v2 almost-prime statement, it cuts neither way on the conjecture.
events.object: Existence claim: the title asserts that some quadratic polynomial represents infinitely many primes. The readable pages name no explicit polynomial. Whether the existence argument is valid could not be checked, since the full text was not readable to me.

events.what_happened: Runbo Li, 'On the largest prime factor of quadratic polynomials' (arXiv:2406.07575). Shows that the Grimmelt-Merikoski result gives that the largest prime factor of n^2+1 exceeds x^1.317 infinitely often.
events.delivers: A statement about the largest prime factor of n^2+1 (almost-prime size), not about whether n^2+1 is prime. This is a different question sharing the Landau-problem namesake; it settles nothing about prime values.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, including n^2+1 prime infinitely often.
events.direction: Neighbouring result on a different question; neither cuts for nor against the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Stanley Yao Xiao, 'Prime values of f(a,b^2) and f(a,p^2), f quadratic', Algebra & Number Theory 18(9) (2024), pp. 1619-1679, published 19 Sep 2024 (from the journal page I read). It proves an asymptotic formula for primes of the shapes f(a,b^2) and f(a,p^2), with f an irreducible binary quadratic form with no local obstructions.
events.revisions: Journal publication 19 Sep 2024. The first arXiv or other posting date was not checked, so the month and whether the first posting falls before the window are unknown.
events.delivers: Prime values of a binary quadratic form evaluated at squares, with an asymptotic formula. This is a different question: it is about a two-variable form at square arguments, not the univariate conjecture.
events.direction: Neighbouring result on a different question; neither cuts for nor against the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Dan Ismailescu and Yunkyu James Lee, 'Polynomially growing integer sequences all whose terms are composite' (arXiv:2501.04851). The introduction calls Bouniakowsky's conjecture 'still wide open' and says 'to date, the only case of Bouniakowsky's conjecture that can be rigorously proved is that of linear polynomials'. The paper's own results concern finiteness of primes in sequences floor(n^t/d).
events.delivers: Nothing on the conjecture. Its results concern sequences floor(n^t/d); the introduction records the conjecture as open with only the linear case proved. This is a later paper that still calls the problem open and does not claim progress on it.
events.direction: Status statement only: treats the conjecture as open.

events.what_happened: Angelot Behajaina, Pierre Debes and Joachim Konig, 'Integrally Hilbertian rings and the polynomial Schinzel hypothesis' (arXiv:2502.09959). Proves a polynomial version of Schinzel's hypothesis: when Z is replaced by an integrally Hilbertian ring, the statement holds for the polynomial ring Z[U], with 'prime' replaced by 'irreducible'. The abstract says a further conclusion has 'noteworthy consequences' for the classical Schinzel hypothesis, but does not claim to prove it; that conclusion was not readable to me.
events.revisions: v1 14 Feb 2025; v2 8 Apr 2026 (current), per arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Polynomial Schinzel hypothesis in the ring Z[U] with irreducibility in place of primality. This is an analogue (the integers are replaced by a polynomial ring), so it does not settle the integer-ring problem. The consequence it draws for the classical hypothesis was not verified.
events.remains: The integer-ring problem as stated, i.e. all of problem_asks.
events.direction: Analogue in a different ring; neither cuts for nor against the integer conjecture as stated.

events.what_happened: Lasse Grimmelt and Jori Merikoski, 'On the greatest prime factor and uniform equidistribution of quadratic polynomials' (arXiv:2505.00493). Shows that the greatest prime factor of n^2+h is at least n^1.312 infinitely often.
events.delivers: A statement about the greatest prime factor of n^2+h (almost-prime size). It does not claim that n^2+1 is prime infinitely often, so it settles nothing about prime values.
events.direction: Neighbouring result on a different question; neither cuts for nor against the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Abdeslam Aabidi El Moussati, 'Symbolic Resolution of the Bunyakovsky Conjecture via AION', Cambridge Open Engage working paper (DOI 10.33774/coe-2025-2xzb0), version 1 posted 29 May 2025. Abstract (paraphrased from the page; the full abstract exceeds the quote limit): claims a 'structural and symbolic resolution'; primes are defined by inability to be built from earlier symbolic elements through multiplication, in an 'AION irreducibility model'; polynomials that are irreducible, have positive leading term and no fixed divisor 'escape all symbolic multiplicative constructions infinitely often', which the paper says 'guarantees irreducibility in the AION system and therefore infinitely many prime outputs'; says no probabilistic or analytic tools are needed. The page states the content 'has not been peer-reviewed by Cambridge University Press at the time of posting'.
events.revisions: v1 29 May 2025; no later version found.
events.delivers: As claimed, the full conjecture for all f satisfying the three conditions. The abstract does not argue the step from the symbolic property to infinitely many prime values; it asserts it. It also redefines primality through the framework, so as posted it may answer a different question from the one the bullet asks (ordinary primes).
events.remains: Nothing, if the argument held. As posted, I found no checkable argument connecting the stated property to prime values.
events.doubts: (1) The decisive step is asserted, not argued in the abstract. (2) Not peer-reviewed, per the publisher's own page. (3) It redefines primality through the framework ('redefines primality through deterministic symbolic structure'), which may change the question. (4) The same author's series titles appear in search results and claim resolutions of many famous problems: 'Symbolic Resolution of Goldbach's Conjecture via the AION Framework', 'Symbolic Resolution of the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture via Irreducible Ancestry in AION', 'A Formal Resolution of the Beal Conjecture via Symbolic Ancestry and Arithmetic Embedding'; the search summary also reports a Riemann Hypothesis claim in an 'AION' paper. I did not open those. (5) No mathematician's response was found.
events.direction: Claims to prove the conjecture for all degrees, by a framework that redefines primality. Whether that cuts for the conjecture as stated depends on whether the redefinition is harmless, which the abstract does not establish.

events.what_happened: Huan Xiao, 'From Golomb to Schinzel', Preprints.org, listed as posted 9 June 2025 (DOI 10.20944/preprints202505.0651.v2; the listing I saw is for the second version). Per a search listing, it claims to prove Schinzel's hypothesis using Golomb's method, and is labelled a not-peer-reviewed version under CC BY 4.0. I could not open the manuscript: every Preprints.org URL I tried returned HTTP 403. The description rests on search snippets, not the paper.
events.revisions: Listing shows the v2 DOI; the v1 date was not checked.
events.delivers: As claimed, Schinzel's hypothesis H for all finite systems of irreducible polynomials. Wikipedia identifies Bunyakovsky's conjecture as a special case of Schinzel's hypothesis H, so a valid proof of the claim would settle this problem for every degree. Whether the argument covers single polynomials of degree at least 2, and whether it has any restriction, could not be read.
events.remains: As claimed, nothing. If the argument covers less than claimed, all of problem_asks for degree at least 2 remains open.
events.time_since_posted: About 16 months (posted 9 June 2025), with no critique, comment or citation found.
events.doubts: (1) Unrefereed Preprints.org posting claiming a full proof of a famous open problem; Wikipedia (last revised 19 Dec 2025) and the Schinzel Wikipedia page (last edited 7 Oct 2026) still list only the degree-1 case as proved. (2) A CNRS note by Tanguy Rivoal on Golomb's method, seen only as a search snippet (its PDF was unreadable to me), reportedly says Schinzel's conjecture 'seems completely out of reach' outside the degree-1 case because its proof would also imply infinitely many twin primes, and that Golomb's method does not apply as elegantly here. (3) The author's later preprints apply the same method to Bateman-Horn (31 Dec 2025) and Chowla (5 Jan 2026), a breadth that is itself a reason for caution. (4) Affiliation 'School of Artificial Intelligence, Zhuhai City Polytechnic' comes from a search summary and is unverified; the identity of the author was not confirmed.
events.direction: Claims to prove the general Schinzel statement, so as claimed it cuts for the conjecture in every degree, including the single-polynomial case.

events.what_happened: Doherty Andrade, 'Polynomials generating prime numbers' (title as translated in a search summary), Jornal Eletronico de Ensino e Pesquisa de Matematica (JEEPEMA) 9(1) (2025), pp. 92-108, in Portuguese. An expository article: it frames the Bunyakovsky conjecture with its three conditions, says the conjecture is still unrefuted as of 2024, cites Deloin (2020), and includes Ulam and Sacks spirals with Python code. I could not read the PDF (binary), so these details come from search snippets.
events.delivers: None found: expository, and the snippets I saw claim no new result on the conjecture.
events.doubts: The article's account of Deloin's approach and the community's reservations rests on search snippets I could not verify.
events.direction: Status statement only, treating the conjecture as open.

events.what_happened: Noah Kravitz, Katharine Woo and Max Wenqiang Xu, 'The distribution of prime values of random polynomials' (arXiv:2512.03292). Abstract: 'We show that 100% of polynomials (in an L^k sense for all k) satisfy the Bateman-Horn Conjecture', with averaging over the coefficients exponential in the size of the inputs; also Poisson-distributed gaps between prime values for 100% of polynomials.
events.revisions: v1 only, submitted 2 Dec 2025, per arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: An averaged statement about almost all polynomials in an averaged sense. It does not establish the conclusion for any particular f, and so does not settle the bullet as stated, which is a claim about each admissible f.
events.remains: Every individual f, i.e. all of problem_asks.
events.direction: Averaged support for the Bateman-Horn statement, which includes the Bunyakovsky infinitude claim; neither proves nor refutes any particular f.

events.what_happened: Huan Xiao, 'From Golomb to Bateman-Horn', Preprints.org, listed as posted 31 Dec 2025 (DOI 10.20944/preprints202512.2666.v1), labelled a not-peer-reviewed version. Per a search listing it claims to prove the Bateman-Horn conjecture using Golomb's method. Not opened (Preprints.org returned HTTP 403 for the manuscript URL).
events.delivers: As claimed, the Bateman-Horn conjecture in general. Bateman-Horn is the quantitative form that includes the infinitude statement for each admissible f, so a valid proof would cover this problem. Scope and restrictions could not be read.
events.remains: As claimed, nothing; otherwise all of problem_asks.
events.doubts: Same grounds as xiao-2025-golomb-schinzel: unrefereed, a claimed proof of a famous open problem, the Hindry-Rivoal snippet on Golomb's method, and the author's pattern of parallel claims. Bateman-Horn is a stronger statement than the conjecture here, so a claim of it is a larger claim.
events.direction: Claims the Bateman-Horn conjecture, which would cut for this problem if valid.

events.what_happened: Huan Xiao, 'From Bateman-Horn to Chowla', Preprints.org, listed as posted 5 Jan 2026 (DOI 10.20944/preprints202601.0277.v1), labelled not peer-reviewed. Per a search listing it claims a parallel proof of Chowla's conjecture on the Liouville function by the Bateman-Horn method. Not opened.
events.delivers: Nothing on this problem. It concerns Chowla's conjecture on the Liouville function, a different conjecture; recorded because it is by the same author and method.
events.doubts: Unrefereed, and not opened. Its relevance to this problem is only through the shared method.
events.direction: Neighbouring claim on a different conjecture; neither cuts for nor against this problem.

events.what_happened: Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository, file FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/Bunyakovsky.lean (copyright 2025 'The Formal Conjectures Authors', Apache 2.0). It formalises the problem as a single theorem, annotated '@[category research open, AMS 11]', with the proof left as sorry: theorem bunyakovsky_conjecture (f : Z[X]) : BunyakovskyCondition f and SchinzelCondition {f} implies Infinite {n : N | (f.eval n).natAbs.Prime}. The docstring cites the Wikipedia article. No individual author or commit date was named; the file's copyright year is 2025, and the exact commit date was not checked.
events.delivers: Nothing toward a result: a formal statement of the conjecture with its proof left as sorry. Its hypothesis adds that the Schinzel condition holds for {f}, and it quantifies over natural numbers n, including 0, using the absolute value of f(n). Those are fidelity details for a later pass; they do not change the content.
events.direction: A formal statement of the conjecture; it neither proves nor refutes it.

summary: The problem's status is as Wikipedia describes it: open for every f of degree at least 2, with only the degree-1 case (Dirichlet) proved. Wikipedia's Bunyakovsky page was last revised 19 Dec 2025 and lists no claimed proof; the Schinzel hypothesis page, which names Bunyakovsky's conjecture as its single-polynomial case, was last edited 7 Oct 2026 and still lists only the degree-1 case. Since 26 Jan 2024 I found no checked resolution, no counterexample and no case of degree 2 or higher settled. The in-window events are: (a) a May 2025 'symbolic resolution' by Abdeslam Aabidi El Moussati (Cambridge Open Engage), not peer-reviewed, whose abstract asserts the decisive step without argument and redefines primality; (b) Huan Xiao's June 2025 Preprints.org claim to prove Schinzel's hypothesis by Golomb's method, which would settle this problem if valid (Bunyakovsky is the single-polynomial case of Schinzel's hypothesis, per Wikipedia), but whose text I could not open (HTTP 403), so its scope and argument are unverified; and (c) Xiao's December 2025 and January 2026 claims of Bateman-Horn and Chowla by the same method, also unopened. No review, critique or citation of any of these surfaced in the searches. Pre-window, the only claimed degree-2 proof is Valerii Sopin's EasyChair preprint 8203 (first version 7 Jun 2022, last 20 Nov 2023). Its scope shifted between versions: the v2 note describes a weaker almost-prime statement for n^2+1, and its full text was unreadable to me, so I could not settle what it proves. Close calls, both readings: (1) Whether Xiao's Schinzel claim counts as an in-window resolution. On its own abstract-level description it does, but the paper was not read; if the argument covers only special classes or averaged statements, it does not. (2) Whether Sopin's preprint counts. Its abstract claims a degree-2 case, which would be a resolution if correct, but it predates the window, has no in-window engagement, and its final version's content is unverified. Neighbouring in-window work (Li 2024 and Grimmelt-Merikoski 2025 on the largest prime factor of n^2+1; Stanley Yao Xiao 2024 on f(a,b^2)) answers different questions, and averaged results (Kravitz-Woo-Xu, Dec 2025; Bateman-Horn on average) hold for almost all polynomials and do not settle any particular f. Behajaina-Debes-Konig (Feb 2025, rev. Apr 2026) prove the polynomial-ring analogue over Z[U] with irreducibles for primes, which does not cover the integer case. The Deloin 2020 proof is known only second-hand, through a 2025 Portuguese expository article (Andrade, JEEPEMA) whose PDF was unreadable to me; I could not locate Deloin's paper or check its scope. AI involvement: no source I could read names an AI system for this problem. 'AION' is a symbolic framework, not an AI system, and the Cambridge page has only competing-interest and ethics statements. Xiao's 'School of Artificial Intelligence' affiliation is not AI involvement, and Xiao's Preprints.org papers could not be opened to check their disclosures. OpenAI's August 2026 'Astra' announcement (ten results, secondary lists) and AxiomProver's 2026 results (secondary lists) do not include this problem; the OpenAI primary page returned HTTP 403. The Google DeepMind formal-conjectures file Bunyakovsky.lean states the problem with its proof left as sorry (one occurrence), so it is a formal statement, not a result.
competing_reading: The strongest case against 'nothing happened' is Xiao's June 2025 claim. If valid, it is the only in-window event that settles the problem outright, since Wikipedia identifies this conjecture as the single-polynomial case of Schinzel's hypothesis. The strongest case for treating it as nothing is the total absence of engagement in about 16 months, the absence of any readable argument in my sources, and the Rivoal snippet calling Schinzel's hypothesis out of reach beyond degree 1. A later pass could reasonably give the in-window claims no weight until the full text is checked, or could count Xiao's claim as a full resolution once it is read.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of Xiao's 'From Golomb to Schinzel' (DOI 10.20944/preprints202505.0651.v2): whether it proves the single-polynomial case of degree at least 2, under what hypotheses, and where the analytic step lies; plus any Preprints.org comment thread. (2) Any referee report, expert review or citation of that paper. (3) A readable copy of Sopin's EasyChair preprint 8203, v4: which statement it proves, whether the shifted or quadratic polynomial is named, and whether Friedlander-Iwaniec is applied correctly; plus any in-window citation or review. (4) The full AION preprint and any mathematician's response. (5) Deloin's 2020 paper itself, with its venue and date. (6) The Rivoal/Hindry note on Golomb's method, readable in full.
